title: DID THE BIBLE FORCE A RAPE VICTIM TO MARRY HER ATTACKER? THE DISTURBING VERSE THAT DESERVES MORE THAN A QUICK ANSWER
paragraphs: DID THE BIBLE FORCE A RAPE VICTIM TO MARRY HER ATTACKER? THE DISTURBING VERSE THAT DESERVES MORE THAN A QUICK ANSWER

Deuteronomy 22:28–29 has been used to accuse God of defending sexual violence. But when we examine the original Hebrew, the surrounding laws, and the heart of Jesus Christ, a more complicated—and deeply important—story emerges.
What if the Bible passage that made you question God's goodness was never explained to you carefully in the first place?
Imagine a young woman whose life has just been shattered.

Something happened that she never wanted. Someone crossed a boundary that should never have been crossed. And now, instead of finding protection, she hears someone open a Bible and tell her that God once commanded a woman in her situation to marry the very man who violated her.
Imagine what those words would do to her.
The confusion. The anger. The sickening thought that perhaps even heaven had taken the side of the man who hurt her.
Now imagine someone telling her she should stop asking questions because questioning Scripture means questioning God.
But what if her question is exactly the kind we need to take seriously?
What if defending the Bible does not require defending every interpretation people have attached to it?
And what if the most faithful response is neither to dismiss the troubling words nor to pretend the ancient world was more compassionate than it actually was?
There is a passage in Deuteronomy that has caused generations of debate, pain, and misunderstanding.
And we need to talk about it.
Not because God's Word needs rescuing from honest questions.
But because people deserve more than careless answers when those answers touch their deepest wounds.
Especially those who have survived sexual violence.
Because behind this debate is something far more personal than an argument about ancient law.
It is a question that can keep a wounded person awake at night.
Does God really care about what happened to me?
And before we finish, we need to let Scripture—not our assumptions—answer that question.
Deuteronomy 22:28–29 reads in the King James Version:
"If a man find a damsel that is a virgin, which is not betrothed, and lay hold on her, and lie with her, and they be found;
Then the man that lay with her shall give unto the damsel's father fifty shekels of silver, and she shall be his wife; because he hath humbled her, he may not put her away all his days."
Read that slowly.
A man takes hold of an unmarried young woman, lies with her, pays her father fifty shekels, and is required to marry her.
There is no need to pretend that those words sound comfortable to modern ears.
They don't.
And the disturbing question is understandable.
Was the woman being punished for what the man did?
Was marriage being used to protect an attacker?
Was a victim being denied the freedom to refuse?
Those are serious questions. And they deserve serious answers.

But before anyone announces that the Bible clearly commands rape victims to marry their attackers—or insists that the passage could not possibly involve sexual assault—we must examine what the Hebrew text actually says.
Because the truth is more complicated than either slogan.
The key Hebrew expression in Deuteronomy 22:28 is:
וּתְפָשָׂהּ וְשָׁכַב עִמָּהּ
Utefasah veshakhav immah.
A close rendering is: "and he seizes/takes hold of her and lies with her."
The verb תָּפַשׂ (taphas) can mean to seize, grasp, catch, capture, or take hold of something or someone.
It does not automatically mean rape in every context.
But neither does it automatically mean a gentle, consensual encounter.
That distinction matters enormously.

Some interpreters argue that Deuteronomy 22:28–29 concerns seduction or illicit intercourse rather than forcible rape. Others understand the language of taking hold of the woman, together with the legal consequences, as describing sexual assault.
Both positions have been defended by serious interpreters.
And the Hebrew verb alone cannot settle the dispute.
That is where many popular explanations go wrong.
They take one word, assign it one preferred meaning, and act as though the entire controversy has disappeared.
But faithful Bible study requires more patience than that.
Now look at the verses immediately before it.
Deuteronomy 22:25–27 describes a man who finds a betrothed woman in the countryside and forces himself upon her.
The Hebrew uses a different verb:
וְהֶחֱזִיק־בָּהּ
Vehecheziq-bah.
This conveys the idea of taking hold of her or overpowering her.
And the passage says something unmistakable.
The woman is not to be punished.
Deuteronomy 22:26 declares:
"But unto the damsel thou shalt do nothing; there is in the damsel no sin worthy of death."
Then Scripture compares what happened to her with murder.
"For as when a man riseth against his neighbour, and slayeth him, even so is this matter."
Do not rush past that.
In this particular case, the law does not blame the woman for the violence committed against her.
It explicitly declares her innocent.
And it compares the attack to a grave act of violence.
That matters.
It means that anyone claiming the Mosaic law always treated women who experienced sexual assault as guilty is ignoring an important part of the text.
But there is another detail.
The woman in verses 25–27 is betrothed.
The woman in verses 28–29 is not.
And in the ancient Israelite legal system, betrothal was not merely the equivalent of modern dating or engagement. It established a legally binding marital relationship.
That distinction affects how the laws are organized.
The surrounding legislation addresses different situations involving marriage status, sexual wrongdoing, family obligations, and legal penalties.
We must not flatten those differences.
But neither should we use those differences to erase the difficult questions about the unmarried woman in verses 28–29.
Here is where the debate becomes especially important.
Exodus 22:16–17 describes another situation:
"And if a man entice a maid that is not betrothed, and lie with her, he shall surely endow her to be his wife.
If her father utterly refuse to give her unto him, he shall pay money according to the dowry of virgins."
Notice the word "entice."
The Hebrew verb is פָּתָה (pathah), which in this context conveys enticing or persuading.
It is not the same verb used in Deuteronomy 22:28.
And Exodus explicitly provides for the father to refuse the marriage.
That is significant.
It demonstrates that, in at least one law addressing sexual intercourse with an unbetrothed virgin, marriage was not inevitable.
The man could still owe financial compensation even when the marriage did not take place.

This is one reason some interpreters read Deuteronomy 22:28–29 alongside Exodus 22:16–17 and conclude that the Deuteronomy law also concerns a nonviolent encounter that creates a serious legal obligation for the man.

Others point out that the two passages use different verbs and do not explicitly establish identical circumstances. They therefore caution against assuming that Exodus automatically resolves Deuteronomy.
And there is one more uncomfortable fact we should not hide.
Neither Deuteronomy 22:28–29 nor Exodus 22:16–17 explicitly records the woman's own right to refuse the marriage.
Exodus mentions the father's refusal.
That is not the same thing as the woman's consent.
We cannot simply insert her expressed consent into the passage and then claim that the Hebrew explicitly says it.
It doesn't.
And that honesty is essential.
Because if we have to add words that are not there in order to make the Bible easier to defend, we have already abandoned careful interpretation.
This is where we must understand something about the ancient world.
Marriage, inheritance, family honor, economic security, and sexual relations were governed by social arrangements dramatically different from those familiar to many readers today.
An unmarried woman's prospects could be severely affected by the loss of virginity, regardless of whether she had willingly participated.
That reality was often deeply unfair to women.
And the law in Deuteronomy places a financial obligation on the man and prevents him from later divorcing the woman.
In that social setting, such provisions could function as constraints on male irresponsibility and attempts to abandon a woman after intercourse.
But we must be careful.
Explaining the historical purpose of a law is not the same as proving that every consequence was good for every woman affected by it.
A compulsory marriage to a violent man would not become safe merely because he was forbidden to divorce her.
And financial compensation to a father is not equivalent to healing, justice, or restored dignity for the woman herself.
We should never confuse the existence of a legal remedy with the complete restoration of the person who suffered.
That distinction is vital.
Especially for someone who has experienced abuse and has been told that maintaining a relationship matters more than personal safety.
Scripture must never be weaponized to demand that someone remain exposed to sexual violence.
The passage is not a command to modern rape survivors to marry their attackers.
Nor is it a justification for coercing a victim into marriage today.

Whatever conclusion one reaches about the precise offense addressed in Deuteronomy 22:28–29, applying that ancient Israelite civil law as a universal marriage requirement for victims of sexual assault would ignore its historical and covenantal setting.
And Christians have an even greater responsibility.
We must read Scripture in the light of its unfolding revelation, culminating in Jesus Christ.
Not by pretending the Old Testament never existed.
Not by cutting out difficult passages.
But by asking how the whole biblical story leads us toward God's redemptive purposes.
Jesus Himself teaches that certain provisions in the Mosaic law must be understood in relation to the hardness of human hearts.
When questioned about divorce, He says in Matthew 19:8:
"Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so."
Jesus was speaking specifically about divorce.
We should not pretend He was directly interpreting Deuteronomy 22:28–29.
But His words establish an important principle.
Not every legal provision regulating life in a fallen society represents the fullest expression of God's original design for human relationships.
Sometimes biblical law addresses the realities of human sin in a world already damaged by it.
And that brings us to something many people overlook.
The Bible does not always describe the world as it should be. Sometimes it shows us how deeply the world needs redemption.
Think about that.
The Bible contains slavery, betrayal, war, sexual violence, exploitation, injustice, and cruelty.
Not because every recorded action receives divine approval.
But because Scripture tells the truth about a broken humanity.
It refuses to hide the darkness.
And one of the most devastating examples appears in 2 Samuel 13.
A young woman named Tamar is violated by her half-brother Amnon.
The account does not romanticize what happened.
It does not describe the assault as love.
Tamar protests. She pleads. She reasons with him.
But he refuses to listen.
And after the assault, he despises her.
The man who claimed to desire her now treats her as disposable.
Tamar is left devastated.
Second Samuel 13:19 describes her tearing her garment, putting ashes on her head, and crying aloud.
It is one of the most heartbreaking scenes in the Old Testament.
And if you have ever wondered whether Scripture understands the cruelty of sexual violation, read Tamar's story.
Read her words.
Listen to her protest.
Watch the aftermath.
The Bible does not present Amnon as a hero.
It exposes his wickedness.
And it records the terrible consequences of his actions and the failures of those around Tamar.
But there is another tragedy in that chapter.
Tamar's suffering is not resolved with a neat, comforting ending.
Her story does not give us the kind of closure we wish she had received.
And that is painfully familiar to many survivors.
Sometimes the person who caused the harm continues with life while the wounded person carries memories nobody else can see.
Sometimes family members respond badly.
Sometimes the people who should protect the vulnerable remain silent.
Sometimes justice is delayed or mishandled.
The Bible knows that world.
And Jesus entered it.
Not as a distant observer.
Not as a religious leader who cared more about appearances than wounded people.
But as the Son of God who came to confront sin, reveal the Father, and bring redemption.
Look at how Jesus treated women who had been publicly shamed.
In John 4, He speaks with a Samaritan woman whose personal history had become entangled with broken relationships.
He does not pretend her life has no moral or spiritual significance.
But neither does He treat her as a disposable object.
He speaks to her with dignity.
He reveals Himself to her.
And the woman who came to draw water becomes someone who tells others about Him.
Look at Luke 7, where a woman known publicly as a sinner approaches Jesus with tears.
Others see her reputation.
Jesus sees her faith and her love.
He speaks of forgiveness.
And He refuses to let the contempt of the room determine her worth.
These accounts are not identical to the experience of a rape survivor, and we should never imply that someone who has been assaulted is guilty of sexual sin because of what another person did.
That distinction must remain absolutely clear.
Sexual assault is not the victim's sin.
A person does not become morally defiled by being violated against their will.
The shame belongs to the wrongdoing, not to the person who was harmed.
And no survivor should be pressured to confess guilt for someone else's violence.
The Gospel does not require that.
Jesus does not require that.
And neither should His Church.
Perhaps this is the moment when the discussion stops being merely historical.
Because there may be someone reading this who knows exactly what it means to carry a wound that other people have mishandled.
Maybe you told someone what happened, and they asked what you were wearing.
Maybe you spoke up, and someone told you to keep quiet for the family's reputation.
Maybe you were pressured to forgive before anyone acknowledged the truth.
Maybe someone used Bible verses to make you feel responsible for protecting the person who hurt you.
Maybe you were told that reporting abuse would damage the church.
And maybe, after all that, you began wondering whether God was as indifferent as the people who claimed to represent Him.
Please hear this.
The failures of people who speak in God's name are not proof that they have represented God's heart faithfully.
The God revealed in Scripture commands justice.
Psalm 82:3–4 says:
"Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy.
Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked."
Isaiah 1:17 commands God's people to seek justice, relieve the oppressed, and defend the vulnerable.
And Jesus condemns religious hypocrisy that neglects the weightier matters of the law, including judgment, mercy, and faithfulness (Matthew 23:23).
Those are not small themes.
They are woven throughout Scripture.
God's people are not called to protect powerful wrongdoers from accountability.
They are called to love truth, pursue justice, protect the vulnerable, and walk humbly before Him.
And protecting someone from further abuse is not a betrayal of forgiveness.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending a crime never happened.
It does not automatically restore trust.
It does not eliminate the need for accountability.
And it does not require a survivor to return to an unsafe relationship.
Repentance matters.
Justice matters.
Truth matters.
Safety matters.
And so does the wounded person whom everyone else may have forgotten.
Now return to Deuteronomy 22.
Can we confidently say that the passage never concerned rape?
No. The language and interpretive debate do not justify that certainty.
Can we confidently say that it explicitly commanded every rape victim to marry her attacker?
No. That sweeping claim goes beyond what the passage establishes.
Can we say that Exodus 22:16–17 includes a provision allowing the father to refuse marriage?
Yes.
Can we say that Deuteronomy 22:25–27 explicitly protects the innocence of the assaulted betrothed woman?
Yes.
Can we say that the woman's own consent is explicitly addressed in Deuteronomy 22:28–29?
No.
And can we honestly acknowledge that the legal arrangements of ancient Israel raise difficult moral questions for modern readers?
Absolutely.
Faith does not become stronger by pretending hard questions do not exist.
Sometimes faith grows deeper when we refuse easy answers and keep seeking the truth.
The Hebrew text matters.
The ancient legal context matters.
The differences between the passages matter.
The historical treatment of women matters.
And the testimony of those who have suffered matters.
None of those should be discarded simply because they complicate an argument.
But there is something else we must remember.
The center of Christianity is not a claim that every ancient social institution was perfect.
The center of Christianity is Jesus Christ.
The One who entered a fallen world.
The One who exposed hypocrisy.
The One who called sinners to repentance.
The One who welcomed the brokenhearted.
The One who gave His life for our redemption.
And the One who rose again.
At the cross, we see both the seriousness of evil and the astonishing mercy of God.
Jesus did not come to tell humanity that sin was harmless.
He came because sin is devastating.
It destroys trust.
It exploits weakness.
It corrupts power.
It fractures families.
It leaves wounds that human beings cannot simply erase.
And yet the Gospel declares that evil will not have the final word.
Through Christ, forgiveness is offered to repentant sinners.
Through Christ, the wounded are invited to receive grace.
Through Christ, the broken can find hope.
Through Christ, the Church is called to become a community of truth, justice, compassion, holiness, and restoration.
That does not mean every survivor will immediately feel healed.
It does not mean memories disappear overnight.
It does not mean the consequences of abuse cease to exist.
And it certainly does not mean victims owe their attackers access to their lives.
But it does mean that what happened to a person does not determine their ultimate worth before God.
Their dignity is not destroyed by another person's sin.
Their future is not owned by their attacker.
Their story is not finished because someone else wrote a terrible chapter.
And their pain is not invisible to the Lord.
Psalm 34:18 says:
"The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit."
Those words do not promise that every wound will vanish today.
They promise something far more personal.
God is not indifferent to the brokenhearted.
We mean that evil does not possess the authority to define the ending of a life surrendered to Christ.
We mean that grace is not the denial of what happened.
Grace is God's power to meet us in the truth of what happened and lead us toward redemption.
We mean that the Gospel does not erase justice.
It calls us to take sin seriously while trusting the Savior who can redeem what sin has devastated.
And if someone who committed sexual violence is reading this, the call of Christ is not to hide behind religious language.
It is to repent.
To stop harming others.
To acknowledge wrongdoing.
To accept accountability.
To make no demands upon the person harmed.
And to seek the mercy of God without using that mercy as an excuse to escape earthly consequences.
Grace is never permission to continue evil.
And repentance is more than being sorry that the truth came out.
The Gospel calls for a transformed life.
Maybe that is why this difficult passage deserves such careful study.
Because how we interpret Scripture shapes how we treat people.
If we read carelessly, we can wound those who are already suffering.
If we defend our preferred explanations more fiercely than we defend the vulnerable, we may win an argument while failing to demonstrate the love of Christ.
But if we approach God's Word with humility, reverence, intellectual honesty, and compassion, we can begin to see how biblical truth calls us toward both holiness and mercy.
And perhaps someone reading this has been standing at the edge of faith for years.
Not because they hated God.
But because nobody would answer the question that haunted them.
Nobody would acknowledge the complexity.
Nobody would admit that some biblical passages are genuinely difficult.
Nobody would sit beside them long enough to say, "Your question deserves a careful answer."
If that is you, please do not mistake a careless explanation of Scripture for the fullness of Scripture itself.
Keep reading.
Keep asking.
Keep examining the text.
And above all, keep looking at Jesus Christ.
Because the Christian faith is not an invitation to shut down your conscience.
It is an invitation to follow the One who is the truth.
And truth has nothing to fear from honest examination.
If this article helped you understand something you once feared to question, I would love to hear what stood out to you.
Or share, in your own words, what you think Christians most need to understand about this passage.
You do not have to disclose a personal trauma or reveal anything you are not comfortable sharing.
And if you are still wrestling with the text, you are welcome in the conversation too.
A thoughtful question is worth more than a hundred confident answers that refuse to listen.
If you know someone who has walked away from Christianity because of difficult Bible passages, consider sharing this article directly with them.
Not to pressure them.
Not to win an argument.
But to let them know that serious questions deserve serious study.
Because the world does not need more Christians who are merely loud.
It needs Christians who know the Word, love the truth, defend the vulnerable, and reflect the character of Jesus.
That is part of why Gospel Warrior exists.

These resources are intended to help believers grow in biblical understanding, strengthen their faith, and walk more faithfully with Jesus Christ.
And we want that work to continue reaching more people.
It is a voluntary act of financial partnership that helps sustain the work, support ongoing teaching, develop new resources, and expand our ability to reach people with the Gospel.
That is our way of expressing gratitude to those who help make this ministry possible.
You can still participate in the mission.
Read the free resources.
Share the teaching.
Pray for the ministry.
Encourage someone who is struggling.
And keep growing in the Word.
Because the Gospel is not for sale.
God's love cannot be purchased.
There are people who have been wounded by sin.
People who have been wounded by careless religious teaching.
People who have questions they are afraid to ask.
People who are spiritually exhausted.
People who are one honest conversation away from reconsidering the Jesus they thought they knew.
They do not need us to manipulate them.
They need us to tell the truth.
They need us to handle God's Word faithfully.
They need us to love people without compromising holiness.
And they need us to keep pointing beyond ourselves to the crucified and risen Savior.
So return to the question that began this conversation.
Did the Bible force a rape victim to marry her attacker?

The most responsible answer is that Deuteronomy 22:28–29 is a genuinely debated ancient law. Its Hebrew wording, relationship to Exodus 22:16–17, and implications for consent require careful interpretation. It should not be simplified into an unqualified claim that God commanded all rape victims to marry their attackers, nor should its troubling features be dismissed by claiming that the original Hebrew unquestionably describes consensual sex.
We must tell the truth about what we know.
We must acknowledge what remains disputed.
And we must never use an uncertain interpretation to justify the abuse of a vulnerable person.
Because biblical faithfulness is not measured by how quickly we can silence a difficult question.
It is measured, in part, by whether we are willing to seek the truth and obey the God who calls us to justice, mercy, humility, and love.
And to the person who began reading this article with a wound nobody else could see:
What happened to you does not make you less worthy of dignity.
You are not required to call evil good.
You are not required to protect the reputation of someone who harmed you.
And you are not beyond the reach of Christ's compassion.
The road toward healing may be long.
There may be tears, questions, difficult conversations, and days when faith feels fragile.
But your suffering is not a verdict on your worth.
And your story is not over.
The hands that were pierced for our redemption will never ask you to call your wounds a blessing in order to prove that His grace is real.
